RU-B1-01-001.notes: Если бы triggers the past form in both clauses, whatever the time: было, поехал. время is neuter, so было. The conditional has no separate future or present forms.

RU-B1-01-002.notes: The cue tells you the speaker is a woman, so the past form after бы is feminine: пришла. Without context, Russian doesn't mark whether the condition is past or present.

RU-B1-01-003.notes: Я бы хотел is the polite way to say 'I'd like'. A man says хотел; a woman, хотела. It's softer than хочу, which can sound demanding to strangers.

RU-B1-01-004.notes: Если бы + past form gives an unreal condition: если бы ты позвонил. The cue tells you the listener is a man, so -л. Perfective here, because a single call is meant.

RU-B1-01-005.notes: На твоём месте (in your place) sets up an imaginary situation, so бы is needed. бы usually follows the first stressed word or the pronoun, not necessarily the verb.

RU-B1-01-006.notes: если бы + past form follows a main clause that already has бы: было бы хорошо. In если бы, the бы attaches to если rather than the verb, so the clause opens with both words.

RU-B1-01-007.notes: Ты бы + past form is a gentle piece of advice: you ought to, why not. It's softer than тебе надо, and very common in speech.

RU-B1-01-008.notes: A real future condition takes если + future (будет); an unreal one takes если бы + past form (был). дождь is masculine, so был.

RU-B1-02-001.notes: The present active participle replaces который + present: читающий = который читает. It's formed from the они stem (чита-ют) + -ющий and agrees with человек.

RU-B1-02-002.notes: Second-conjugation verbs take -ящий / -ащий: говор-ят → говорящий. девушку is accusative, so the participle is accusative too: говорящую.

RU-B1-02-003.notes: жить has the они form живут, so the participle is живущий; it agrees with студенты in the nominative plural: живущие. Participle phrases are set off by commas.

RU-B1-02-004.notes: The past active participle replaces который + past: написавший = который написал. It's formed from the past stem (написа-) + -вший.

RU-B1-02-005.notes: Reflexive verbs keep -ся after a participle ending, never -сь: вернувшийся. друга is accusative animate, so the participle takes the genitive-like -егося.

RU-B1-02-006.notes: студентка is feminine nominative, so получившая. Past active participles from perfective verbs describe a completed action.

RU-B1-02-007.notes: The short passive participle forms the passive with быть: книга написана. It agrees in gender with the subject (feminine -а) and is stressed like the past form.

RU-B1-02-008.notes: Магазин закрыт is the everyday way to say 'the shop is closed'. закрыть gives the -т participle: закрыт, закрыта, закрыто, закрыты.

RU-B1-02-009.notes: окно is neuter, so открыто. The neuter short form looks like an adverb, and Открыто on a door sign means 'open'.

RU-B1-02-010.notes: билеты is plural, so проданы. Verbs in -ать give -ан: продать → продан, продана, проданы. The long form, проданный, is used before a noun.

RU-B1-02-011.notes: The past passive uses была + the short participle: работа была сделана. Both agree with работа, which is feminine.

RU-B1-02-012.notes: The long past passive participle comes before or after the noun and agrees with it: построенный. -ить verbs take -енный.

RU-B1-02-013.notes: любимый (favourite) began as the present passive participle of любить and is now an ordinary adjective. It agrees with книга: любимая.

RU-B1-02-014.notes: Уважаемые коллеги! is the standard opening of a formal letter or speech. уважаемый is the present passive participle of уважать (respect).

RU-B1-02-015.notes: The present passive participle adds -емый to the мы form: обсуждаем → обсуждаемый. It agrees with проблемы in the plural nominative.

RU-B1-03-001.notes: The imperfective verbal adverb describes an action at the same time as the main verb: читая, он пил. It's formed from the они stem + -я.

RU-B1-03-002.notes: делать gives делая, from дела-ют minus -ют, plus -я. The verbal adverb must share its subject with the main verb (он).

RU-B1-03-003.notes: The perfective verbal adverb describes an action completed before the main one: прочитав, она заплакала. It's formed from the past stem + -в.

RU-B1-03-004.notes: Reflexive verbs take -вшись: вернувшись. The cue tells you the speaker is a man, so лёг. The imperfective form возвращаясь would mean 'while coming back'.

RU-B1-03-005.notes: не + perfective verbal adverb gives 'without doing': не сказав ни слова. ни слова uses the genitive after negation.

RU-B1-03-006.notes: говорить gives говоря, a second-conjugation form with the stress on the ending. It means 'while talking'.

RU-B1-03-007.notes: Simultaneous action takes the imperfective гуляя; a completed earlier action takes the perfective погуляв. The aspect of the verbal adverb carries the time relation.

RU-B1-04-001.notes: нельзя + imperfective means 'not allowed'; нельзя + perfective means 'impossible'. The aspect, not the word нельзя, decides.

RU-B1-04-002.notes: A prohibition takes the imperfective after нельзя: фотографировать. Сфотографировать would mean it's physically impossible.

RU-B1-04-003.notes: Не надо + imperfective means 'there's no need': не надо покупать. With a perfective it would sound like a warning.

RU-B1-04-004.notes: Не нужно, like не надо, takes the imperfective when it means 'no need to'. He shouldn't be called at all.

RU-B1-04-005.notes: Never having done something takes the imperfective: не читал. Failing to finish takes the perfective: не прочитал до конца.

RU-B1-04-006.notes: The imperfective приходил means he came and went (a round trip); the perfective пришёл means he's here now. This annulled-result use is a key aspect contrast.

RU-B1-04-007.notes: The window is shut again, so the result was undone: the imperfective открывал. Открыл would mean it's still open.

RU-B1-04-008.notes: искать has no prefixed perfective; найти (find) is the result verb. наконец goes with the achieved result: нашёл.

RU-B1-04-009.notes: ловить (try to catch) pairs with поймать (catch). The perfective has an irregular stem: поймаю, поймала.

RU-B1-04-010.notes: перестать (stop) always takes an imperfective infinitive: перестал курить. The same is true of бросить in the sense 'give up'.

RU-B1-04-011.notes: надоесть (be fed up with) takes an imperfective infinitive: надоело ждать. It's impersonal: мне надоело.

RU-B1-04-012.notes: привыкнуть (get used to) takes an imperfective infinitive for a habit: привык вставать. Habits are repeated actions.

RU-B1-05-001.notes: One direction now takes the unidirectional нести: несу. The multidirectional носить is for habits or round trips.

RU-B1-05-002.notes: Every day signals a habit, so the multidirectional водить: водит. вести / водить mean 'lead, take on foot'.

RU-B1-05-003.notes: One trip now by car takes the unidirectional везти: везёт. возить is for habits. Its past is вёз, везла, with no -л in the masculine.

RU-B1-05-004.notes: Regular exercise takes the multidirectional бегать: бегает. бежать is one direction, often in a hurry.

RU-B1-05-005.notes: One flight now, in one direction, takes лететь: летит. лететь changes т → ч in the я form: лечу. The multidirectional летать is used for habits and for flying in general.

RU-B1-05-006.notes: General ability takes the multidirectional плавать. плыть means swimming in one direction or a ship sailing somewhere.

RU-B1-05-007.notes: One direction now takes бежать: бежишь. бежать is irregular: бегу, бежишь, бегут. It's one of the few verbs mixing both conjugations.

RU-B1-05-008.notes: часто signals repetition, so the multidirectional летать: летаю. It's a regular first-conjugation verb.

RU-B1-05-009.notes: под- means approaching: подойти к + dative. The past is подошёл, from шёл. The imperfective is подходить: подходит к окну.

RU-B1-05-010.notes: от- means moving a short distance away: отойти от + genitive. A woman says отошла. Compare уйти, which means leaving altogether, not just stepping back.

RU-B1-05-011.notes: пере- means crossing: перейти улицу. The object can be a bare accusative or через + accusative. The imperfective is переходить: переходить улицу.

RU-B1-05-012.notes: про- means passing by: проехать мимо + genitive. It can also mean going too far: проехать остановку (miss your stop).

RU-B1-05-013.notes: до- means reaching a point: дойти до + genitive. за десять минут gives the time taken. The imperfective доходить also means 'dawn on': до меня дошло.

RU-B1-05-014.notes: об- means going around or covering an area: обойти весь город. The prefix becomes обо- before йти. обойти can also mean 'bypass, avoid': обойти проблему.

RU-B1-05-015.notes: при- + нести gives принести (bring): принеси. воды is a partitive genitive: some water. Its imperfective is приносить: приносит.

RU-B1-05-016.notes: от- + везти gives отвезти (take, by vehicle). It means taking somewhere and leaving it there. The on-foot counterpart is отвести: отведи ребёнка в школу.

RU-B1-05-017.notes: вы- + нести gives вынести (carry out): вынеси мусор. вы- is stressed in the perfective. Its imperfective is выносить: выносить мусор.

RU-B1-05-018.notes: у- + нести gives унести (take away): унёс. The masculine past drops -л, like нёс. The feminine is унесла, with -л restored.

RU-B1-05-019.notes: The imperfective of приехать is приезжать: приезжает. всегда (always) signals a repeated event. Note the spelling -зж-, pronounced as a long ж.

RU-B1-05-020.notes: The imperfective present of уйти is уходит. Timetables use the present for scheduled departures, as in English.

RU-B1-06-001.notes: без + genitive: сахар → сахара. A partitive сахару also exists in colloquial speech, but сахара is standard.

RU-B1-06-002.notes: для + genitive: мама → мамы. для marks the beneficiary, unlike the dative recipient after подарить. для is never used for the person something is given to directly.
RU-B1-06-002.text: (A man speaking) Я купил цветы для {{c1::мамы::мама · genitive}}.
RU-B1-06-002.tr: I bought some flowers for Mum.
RU-B1-06-002.flag: dup: replaced Это подарок для друга (near-identical to A2 Это подарок для неё); answer друга → мамы

RU-B1-06-003.notes: после + genitive: работа → работы. После работы is the standard phrase for 'after work'. Its opposite is до + genitive: до работы.

RU-B1-06-004.notes: до + genitive: вечер → вечера. до means 'until' in time and 'as far as' in space. For the end of a range of time, до pairs with с: с утра до вечера.

RU-B1-06-005.notes: около + genitive: дом → дома. около also means 'about, approximately' with numbers: около ста. возле and рядом с are close synonyms.

RU-B1-06-006.notes: кроме + genitive: Иван → Ивана. It means 'except' or 'besides', depending on context. The phrase кроме того means 'besides, moreover'.

RU-B1-06-007.notes: из-за + genitive gives a negative cause: из-за дождя. A positive cause usually takes благодаря + dative.

RU-B1-06-008.notes: против + genitive: этот план → этого плана. The adjective this agrees in the genitive too. Its opposite is за + accusative: я за этот план.

RU-B1-06-009.notes: за + instrumental after a motion verb means going to fetch something: за лекарством. The same pattern gives за хлебом, за водой.
RU-B1-06-009.text: Она пошла в аптеку {{c1::за лекарством::to get medicine (за + instrumental)}}.
RU-B1-06-009.tr: She went to the chemist's for some medicine.
RU-B1-06-009.flag: dup: replaced Я схожу за хлебом (near-identical to B2 Я схожу в магазин за хлебом); answer за хлебом → за лекарством

RU-B1-06-010.notes: платить / заплатить за + accusative: за билет. The thing paid for takes за, the amount is a direct object.

RU-B1-06-011.notes: за + time + до + genitive means 'that long before': за час до начала. The opposite is через час после.

RU-B1-06-012.notes: мимо + genitive: мимо дома. It's used with motion verbs, often with про-. It can also be an adverb with no noun: он прошёл мимо.

RU-B1-06-013.notes: вдоль + genitive: вдоль реки. It's mainly used with movement or position along a line, such as a road, coast or wall. The adverb is also possible: вдоль и поперёк.

RU-B1-06-014.notes: напротив + genitive: напротив школы. On its own, напротив also means 'on the contrary'. The adjective is противоположный, the noun противоположность.

RU-B1-06-015.notes: вокруг + genitive: вокруг озера. озеро is neuter, so -а in the genitive. It's also an adverb: вокруг никого не было.

RU-B1-06-016.notes: через + accusative means 'across' with motion: через улицу. With перейти, the preposition is optional.

RU-B1-06-017.notes: Saying 'on' a date uses the ordinal in the genitive: пятого марта. The month is also genitive. The year, if added, is genitive too: пятого марта 2020 года.

RU-B1-06-018.notes: Stating today's date uses the neuter nominative ordinal: первое января. число (date) is the understood neuter noun.

RU-B1-06-019.notes: On a date takes the genitive ordinal: двадцатого июня. The answer to Какого числа? is always genitive.

RU-B1-06-020.notes: Seasons use the instrumental without a preposition: летом, зимой. в лето is impossible. The same applies to весной and осенью.
RU-B1-06-020.tr: The city is stuffy in summer.
RU-B1-06-020.flag: dup: replaced Летом мы ездим на море (also inside A1-09-002)

RU-B1-06-021.notes: Times of day use the instrumental: вечером. It can mean 'in the evening' or 'in the evenings'. For 'this evening', сегодня вечером is used.

RU-B1-06-022.notes: зима gives the instrumental зимой. These forms are now treated as adverbs. Note the ending -ой; -ою is archaic.

RU-B1-06-023.notes: утро gives the instrumental утром. Likewise днём and ночью. For 'tomorrow morning', the adverbs combine: завтра утром, and the same goes for вчера вечером.

RU-B1-06-024.notes: за + accusative with motion; за + instrumental for location. за город / за городом both mean 'out of town'.

RU-B1-06-025.notes: под + accusative with motion; под + instrumental for location. залезть shows motion, сидеть location.

RU-B1-06-026.notes: на + accusative with motion (положи на стол); на + prepositional for location (на столе). The verb class matches: класть / положить with motion, лежать with location.

RU-B1-06-027.notes: Mountain ranges in Russia take на: на Кавказе, на Урале. Foreign ranges usually take в: в Альпах. The genitive with 'from' follows: с Кавказа, из Альп.

RU-B1-06-028.notes: Points of the compass take на: на севере, на юге. в is wrong here. The 'from' form follows: с севера.

RU-B1-06-029.notes: вокзал is a на noun: на вокзале. на also goes with станция and остановка. The 'from' form is с вокзала.

RU-B1-06-030.notes: на + accusative gives the intended length of a stay; the plain accusative gives the actual duration. приехать на неделю vs. жить неделю.

RU-B1-06-031.notes: Lending or borrowing for a period uses на + accusative: на два дня. The time is planned, not measured.

RU-B1-06-032.notes: про + accusative is the colloquial equivalent of о + prepositional: про поездку. It's fine in speech but avoided in formal writing.

RU-B1-06-033.notes: бояться takes the genitive: темноты. For people the accusative is common in speech: боюсь бабушку. The perfective испугаться also takes the genitive.

RU-B1-06-034.notes: учиться + dative means learning a skill or subject: учусь музыке. It's bookish; in speech one says учусь играть.

RU-B1-06-035.notes: готовиться к + dative: к экзамену. The perfective is подготовиться. The noun подготовка takes к too: подготовка к экзамену.

RU-B1-06-036.notes: жаловаться на + accusative: на погоду. The person complained to is dative: жаловаться врачу. The noun жалоба also takes на: жалоба на соседа.

RU-B1-06-037.notes: отличаться от + genitive: от Петербурга. Чем asks for the respect in which they differ. The noun отличие gives в отличие от, 'unlike'.

RU-B1-06-038.notes: ждать takes the genitive with abstract or indefinite objects: ответа. With a specific person or thing, the accusative is used.

RU-B1-07-001.notes: встречаться is reciprocal: meet each other. встречать without -ся takes an object: встречать друга. With a third party, it's встречаться с + instrumental.

RU-B1-07-002.notes: -ся on an imperfective verb can express the passive: дом строится. This is the main way to form a present passive.

RU-B1-07-003.notes: An impersonal -ся verb with the dative means 'I don't feel like / can't': мне не спится. The verb is neuter singular.

RU-B1-07-004.notes: мне хочется is a softer, impersonal 'I feel like'. It's less direct than я хочу. The past is хотелось: мне хотелось пить.

RU-B1-07-005.notes: Как пишется? is the standard way to ask how a word is spelt. The word is the subject. Как это произносится? asks for pronunciation.

RU-B1-07-006.notes: начинать takes an object (I start the lesson); начинаться has none (the lesson starts). English uses the same verb for both.

RU-B1-07-007.notes: открыться is intransitive: the door opened by itself. открыть would need an object. Its imperfective is открываться: магазин открывается в девять.

RU-B1-07-008.notes: вернуть takes an object (return something); вернуться means 'come back'. The -ся form is intransitive.

RU-B1-07-009.notes: A third-person plural verb without a subject means 'people, they' in general: здесь не курят. It's the Russian equivalent of an impersonal passive.

RU-B1-07-010.notes: Мне сказали means 'I was told', with no subject. The verb is plural, though only one person may have spoken.

RU-B1-07-011.notes: Тебя зовут к телефону means 'someone's asking for you on the phone'. зовут here is not the name construction.

RU-B1-07-012.notes: хватать is impersonal and takes the genitive of the thing lacking: не хватает времени. The person goes into the dative.

RU-B1-07-013.notes: The perfective хватить in the past is neuter: не хватило. The thing lacking (денег) is genitive. The present would be не хватает.

RU-B1-07-014.notes: Хватит + imperfective infinitive means 'stop doing that': хватит спорить. It's blunt. Хватит! on its own means 'That's enough!'.

RU-B1-07-015.notes: The past of нет is не было + genitive: не было урока. было is always neuter here. The noun is singular here, but the rule holds for plurals too: не было уроков.

RU-B1-07-016.notes: The future of нет is не будет + genitive: не будет дождя. будет is always singular here. The past would be не было дождя.

RU-B1-07-017.notes: A dative + infinitive question asks what one should do: Что мне делать? There's no modal verb. The same pattern gives Куда нам идти?

RU-B1-07-018.notes: бывать means 'be regularly, visit often': бываю. It's the frequentative of быть and is imperfective only. Я часто бываю в Москве implies repeated trips.

RU-B1-07-019.notes: Так бывает is a set phrase: these things happen. бывает is the он form of бывать. Бывает! alone also means 'It happens'.

RU-B1-07-020.notes: Вы бывали…? asks about any visit in the past: Have you ever been to…? The imperfective is used for experience.

RU-B1-07-021.notes: ничего + не means 'nothing' in a normal sentence. нечего + infinitive means 'there's nothing to do', with the stress on не-.

RU-B1-07-022.notes: никогда + не means 'never'. некогда + infinitive means 'there's no time to'. The stress is on не- in некогда.

RU-B1-07-023.notes: нигде + не means 'nowhere'. негде + infinitive means 'there's nowhere to'. The dative gives the person.

RU-B1-07-024.notes: никто always takes не with the verb: никто не пришёл. Russian requires double negation. Likewise ничего не, нигде не, никогда не.

RU-B1-08-001.notes: -то refers to a specific but unknown person: кто-то. -нибудь refers to anyone at all, often in questions: кто-нибудь.

RU-B1-08-002.notes: A suggestion with no destination fixed takes -нибудь: куда-нибудь. -нибудь is used with imperatives, futures and questions.

RU-B1-08-003.notes: He went to a definite place we don't know: куда-то. -то is used with a past action that really happened.

RU-B1-08-004.notes: An offer of anything at all takes -нибудь: что-нибудь. Хочешь что-то выпить? would sound like a specific drink.

RU-B1-08-005.notes: A specific sound actually heard takes -то: что-то. The cue tells you the speaker is a man: слышал. Я что-нибудь слышал would be odd, as the action really happened.

RU-B1-08-006.notes: ли (whether) follows the word in question: придёт ли. It never begins the clause. The tense of the direct question is kept: придёт.

RU-B1-08-007.notes: есть ли asks whether something exists: есть ли у него время. ли follows есть. The answer could be Да, есть or Нет.

RU-B1-08-008.notes: можно ли asks whether something is allowed: можно ли войти. The infinitive follows. In speech, a direct question also works: Спроси, можно войти?

RU-B1-08-009.notes: если is a condition; ли is 'whether' in an indirect question. Using если for 'whether' is a common English-based error.

RU-B1-08-010.notes: хотя (although) introduces a concessive clause. The main clause can add но for emphasis: хотя…, но….

RU-B1-08-011.notes: несмотря на + accusative means 'despite' a noun: несмотря на дождь. It's written as one word. Its opposite is благодаря + dative: thanks to.

RU-B1-08-012.notes: несмотря на то что introduces a clause: despite the fact that. A comma goes before несмотря, and a second comma can split the phrase before что for emphasis.

RU-B1-08-013.notes: так как (since, as) gives a reason and often begins the sentence. It's more formal than потому что, which can't begin a sentence.
RU-B1-08-013.text: {{c1::Так как::since (formal)}} поезд опаздывал, мы решили взять такси.
RU-B1-08-013.tr: As the train was late, we decided to take a taxi.
RU-B1-08-013.flag: dup: replaced Так как шёл дождь, мы остались дома (near-identical to B1-08-020)

RU-B1-08-014.notes: чем + comparative…, тем + comparative… gives 'the more…, the more…'. Both halves need a comparative.

RU-B1-08-015.notes: пока … не means 'until': пока я не вернусь. The не is not a real negation. Without не, пока means 'while': пока я работал.

RU-B1-08-016.notes: как только (as soon as) takes the future for future events: как только он придёт. English uses the present.

RU-B1-08-017.notes: прежде чем + infinitive means 'before doing': прежде чем отвечать. It's more formal than перед тем как.

RU-B1-08-018.notes: после того как introduces a clause: after he left. после alone takes a noun: после ухода. Its counterpart is до того как: before.

RU-B1-08-019.notes: с тех пор как (since) introduces a clause. The main clause is often in the past perfective. с тех пор on its own means 'since then'.

RU-B1-08-020.notes: так что introduces a result: so we stayed in. It comes after a comma, never at the start of the sentence.

RU-B1-08-021.notes: а то means 'or else, otherwise' and follows an imperative. It's colloquial. In writing, иначе is the neutral equivalent.

RU-B1-08-022.notes: не только…, но и… means 'not only…, but also…'. Both parts are needed, and the comma goes before но. Dropping и makes the sentence sound unfinished.

RU-B1-08-023.notes: либо…, либо… means 'either…, or…'. или…, или… is a more colloquial equivalent. A comma goes before the second либо.

RU-B1-08-024.notes: ни…, ни… means 'neither…, nor…' and needs не with the verb: не знаю ни его, ни её. A comma goes before the second ни.

RU-B1-08-025.notes: По-моему (in my opinion) is set off by a comma. по-твоему and по-вашему follow the same pattern. In writing, на мой взгляд is more formal.

RU-B1-08-026.notes: К сожалению (unfortunately) uses к + dative and is set off by commas. К счастью means 'fortunately'.

RU-B1-09-001.notes: друг друга means 'each other'. Only the second word declines: here it's the accusative object, друга.

RU-B1-09-002.notes: помогать takes the dative, so the second part of друг друга goes into the dative: друг другу. The first part never changes.

RU-B1-09-003.notes: A preposition goes between the two parts: друг о друге. The second part takes the case required. Without the preposition the construction would be ungrammatical.

RU-B1-09-004.notes: поссориться с + instrumental: друг с другом. Again, the preposition splits the phrase. Without друг с другом, они поссорились already implies each other.

RU-B1-09-005.notes: сам (oneself) agrees with the person: сам for a man. It emphasises doing something without help. A woman would say сама; a group, сами.

RU-B1-09-006.notes: A woman says сама. The stress falls on the ending in the feminine and plural. Don't confuse сам with себя, the reflexive object.

RU-B1-09-007.notes: дети is plural, so сами. сам also declines for case: самого, самому. самый (the most) is a different word.

RU-B1-09-008.notes: Каждый день (every day) uses the accusative of time. каждый declines like an adjective and is normally singular; the plural appears with numbers: каждые два дня.

RU-B1-09-009.notes: любой means 'any (you like)': любую книгу. It agrees with the noun in the accusative. It's more emphatic than какой-нибудь.

RU-B1-09-010.notes: всякий means 'all kinds of': всякие вещи. It can also mean 'any': в любом случае = во всяком случае.

RU-B1-09-011.notes: у + он gives у него, with н-; the possessive его never takes н-, even after a preposition: у его сестры.
RU-B1-09-011.tip: у него (him) but у его сестры (his sister).
RU-B1-09-011.text: (A man speaking) Я был у {{c1::него::он · genitive (after у)}}, но не у {{c2::его::his (possessive)}} сестры.
RU-B1-09-011.flag: text: added (A man speaking), as был needs the speaker's gender

RU-B1-09-012.notes: кто-нибудь declines like кто, with -нибудь unchanged: с кем-нибудь. A question about anyone takes -нибудь.

RU-B1-09-013.notes: кто-то declines like кто: кому-то. A specific person, whom I've forgotten, takes -то. забыл кому is a short indirect question.

RU-B1-09-014.notes: не с кем + infinitive means 'no one to … with'. The preposition goes between не and кем. The dative of the person goes first: мне.

RU-B1-09-015.notes: ни с кем + не means 'with no one'. The preposition splits ни and кем, and the verb must be negated. Compare не с кем + infinitive, which means 'no one to'.

RU-B1-09-016.notes: не о чем + infinitive means 'nothing to … about'. беспокоиться о + prepositional = worry about. The stress falls on не-.

RU-B1-09-017.notes: некого + infinitive means 'there's no one to': некого спросить. It has no nominative form, and the stress is on не-. The person who lacks someone goes into the dative: мне некого спросить.

RU-B1-09-018.notes: ни разу + не means 'not once'. It's more emphatic than никогда, and раз is in the genitive after ни. Its opposite, не раз, means 'more than once'.

RU-B1-10-001.notes: два has the instrumental двумя: с двумя друзьями. The noun is in the instrumental plural. три, четыре follow the same pattern: тремя, четырьмя.

RU-B1-10-002.notes: три has the genitive трёх: около трёх часов. When the number is in an oblique case, the noun goes into the plural of that case.

RU-B1-10-003.notes: два has the dative двум: двум друзьям. The noun takes the dative plural. три and четыре give трём and четырём.

RU-B1-10-004.notes: оба has a feminine form обе: обе сестры. Like два, it takes the genitive singular in the nominative.

RU-B1-10-005.notes: оба is used with masculine and neuter nouns: оба брата. The oblique stem is обоих (m., n.) or обеих (f.).

RU-B1-10-006.notes: пять has the genitive пяти: до пяти часов. Numbers from 5 to 20 decline like feminine -ь nouns. Its dative and prepositional are also пяти.

RU-B1-10-007.notes: пять has the instrumental пятью: с пятью друзьями. The stress is on the stem. Numbers ending in -ь all take -ью: десятью, двадцатью.

RU-B1-10-008.notes: After два / три / четыре, a masculine noun is genitive singular, but its adjective goes into the genitive plural: два больших дома.

RU-B1-10-009.notes: With feminine nouns after две / три / четыре, the adjective is usually nominative plural: две большие комнаты. The genitive больших is also correct.

RU-B1-10-010.notes: Masculine nouns after три take an adjective in the genitive plural: три новых студента. With feminine nouns, it would usually be новые: три новые студентки.

RU-B1-10-011.notes: A compound number ending in один takes the nominative singular: двадцать один студент. The last digit decides.

RU-B1-10-012.notes: Ages ending in один take год: двадцать один год. Two, three and four take года; five and above, лет.

RU-B1-10-013.notes: один also means 'alone' and agrees with the person: одна for a woman. The plural одни means 'alone' for groups: мы были одни.

RU-B1-10-014.notes: Plural-only nouns take the plural одни: одни часы. Likewise одни брюки, одни ножницы. With ordinary plurals, одни means 'only, nothing but'.

RU-B1-10-015.notes: In a compound ordinal only the last word declines: двадцать первом. век is masculine, so -ом. In writing it's simply в XXI веке.

RU-B1-10-016.notes: Only the last word of a year declines: девяносто пятом году. The rest stay as cardinals. тысяча девятьсот stays in the nominative.

RU-B1-10-017.notes: без + genitive gives 'to' the hour: без пятнадцати пять (14:45 or 16:45). без четверти is also common.

RU-B1-10-018.notes: в половине + genitive ordinal of the next hour: в половине пятого = at 4:30. Russian counts towards the coming hour.

RU-B1-10-019.notes: Minutes past the hour use the genitive ordinal of the next hour: пять минут шестого = 5:05. In speech, пять ноль пять is also common.

RU-B1-11-001.notes: After сто, человек takes the genitive plural, which is the same as the nominative singular: сто человек. людей is never used after numbers.
RU-B1-11-001.text: В зале было сто {{c1::человек::person · genitive plural after сто}}.
RU-B1-11-001.tr: There were a hundred people in the hall.
RU-B1-11-001.flag: dup: replaced Пришло пять человек (near-identical to C2 Пять человек пришло)

RU-B1-11-002.notes: раз has a genitive plural identical to the nominative: сколько раз. It means 'time' as in occasion. The singular is used after один: один раз.

RU-B1-11-003.notes: носки has the genitive plural носков. Socks, unlike boots or stockings, take a regular -ов. пару носков is the accusative of пара.

RU-B1-11-004.notes: сапоги has a zero genitive plural: сапог. Likewise ботинок, чулок, глаз. The accusative singular is сапог too.

RU-B1-11-005.notes: стулья has the genitive plural стульев. не хватать takes the genitive of what is lacking. The verb is neuter: не хватало.
RU-B1-11-005.text: В зале не хватало {{c1::стульев::стулья · genitive plural}}.
RU-B1-11-005.tr: There weren't enough chairs in the hall.
RU-B1-11-005.flag: dup: replaced У нас нет стульев (near-identical to A1 У нас нет времени)

RU-B1-11-006.notes: деревья has the genitive plural деревьев. много takes the genitive plural. The soft -ьев matches the plural stem деревь-.

RU-B1-11-007.notes: сыновья has the genitive plural сыновей. трое is a collective number used for male people and children.

RU-B1-11-008.notes: Nouns in -анин drop -ин in the plural: англичане, genitive plural англичан. Likewise граждане, граждан.

RU-B1-11-009.notes: гражданин has the plural граждане. Граждане пассажиры! is a public announcement formula. Граждане is formal, used for officials addressing the public.

RU-B1-11-010.notes: имя is a neuter -мя noun with -ен- in the oblique cases: в имени. Only about ten nouns follow this pattern.

RU-B1-11-011.notes: имя has the plural имена, with stressed -а. The genitive plural is имён. Other -мя nouns form the plural the same way: время → времена, знамя → знамёна.

RU-B1-11-012.notes: имя has the genitive plural имён, with a stressed ё. столько takes the genitive plural, like много and сколько. The dative plural is именам.

RU-B1-11-013.notes: коллега is common gender: the agreement follows the person's sex. For a woman: моя коллега. With a man, it's мой коллега.

RU-B1-11-014.notes: умница is common gender and stays the same for a man: он умница. The adjective agrees with the person: большой умница.

RU-B1-11-015.notes: Both the first name and patronymic decline: с Иваном Петровичем. Patronymics in -ович decline like nouns.

RU-B1-11-016.notes: Female names and patronymics decline like feminine nouns: Марии Ивановне. -ия names take -ии. In speech, the patronymic is often shortened: Мариванна.

RU-B1-11-017.notes: A son's patronymic is formed with -ович or -евич: Сергей → Сергеевич. A daughter's would be Сергеевна.

RU-B1-12-001.notes: высокий has the comparative выше, with с → ш. With no чем, the comparison is to something understood.

RU-B1-12-002.notes: близкий has the comparative ближе, with з → ж. ближе к + dative = closer to. The superlative is ближайший.

RU-B1-12-003.notes: дешёвый has the comparative дешевле, with an inserted л. It's an exception to the -ее rule. The superlative is самый дешёвый.

RU-B1-12-004.notes: простой has the comparative проще, with ст → щ. Likewise чистый → чище. проще is also used as an adverb: проще говоря.

RU-B1-12-005.notes: тихий has the comparative тише, with х → ш. The comparative adverb has the same form. The superlative is самый тихий.

RU-B1-12-006.notes: поздно has the comparative позже (also позднее). позже is the normal form in speech. The opposite is раньше.

RU-B1-12-007.notes: лёгкий has the comparative легче, with к → ч, and ё becomes е. It's pronounced лехче, with г / к sounding like х before ч.

RU-B1-12-008.notes: When the second term is a phrase rather than a noun, чем is required: теплее, чем в Москве. The genitive can't be used.

RU-B1-12-009.notes: на + accusative gives the difference: на два года. Without на, the sentence would be ungrammatical. на also gives the difference in amount: на сто рублей дороже.

RU-B1-12-010.notes: comparative + всех gives 'best of all (people)': лучше всех. + всего is used for things: лучше всего.

RU-B1-12-011.notes: Больше всего means 'most of all' about things or activities. Больше всех would compare people. Меньше всего means 'least of all'.

RU-B1-12-012.notes: более + adjective forms the compound comparative: более интересный. It agrees with the noun. менее is the opposite: менее интересный.

RU-B1-12-013.notes: наиболее + adjective forms a formal superlative: наиболее важный. It's typical of written style. In speech, самый is used instead.

RU-B1-12-014.notes: такой же…, как… means 'just as… as…'. такой же agrees with the adjective: такая же умная. The adverb counterpart is так же…, как.

RU-B1-13-001.notes: учиться (study, be a student) is intransitive: учиться в школе. It says where you study, not what. Where you work would be работать в.

RU-B1-13-002.notes: учить + accusative means 'learn, memorise': учу новые слова. учить also means 'teach'. Its perfective is выучить: выучил слова.

RU-B1-13-003.notes: изучать means 'study in depth' and always takes an object: изучает историю. It's used for academic subjects.

RU-B1-13-004.notes: заниматься means 'do one's studies, work' without an object: занимаюсь в библиотеке. With an object it takes the instrumental: заниматься музыкой.

RU-B1-13-005.notes: учить кого + dative means 'teach someone something': учит детей музыке. The pupil is accusative, the subject dative.

RU-B1-13-006.notes: уметь means 'know how to' (a learned skill): умею плавать. мочь means 'be able to' in a specific case.

RU-B1-13-007.notes: мочь means 'can' in the moment: не могу плавать, because of the arm. The skill exists; the possibility doesn't.

RU-B1-13-008.notes: знать means 'know a fact': знаю, где он живёт. It's never followed by an infinitive. For a skill, уметь is used instead.

RU-B1-13-009.notes: поздравлять с + instrumental: с днём рождения. The person congratulated is accusative. The noun is поздравление: поздравление с праздником.

RU-B1-13-010.notes: извиняться перед + instrumental: перед ней. The reason takes за + accusative. The perfective is извиниться.

RU-B1-13-011.notes: зависеть от + genitive: от погоды. Это зависит от… is the standard 'it depends on…'. The adjective is зависимый от.

RU-B1-13-012.notes: надеяться на + accusative: на помощь. With a clause, it's надеяться, что. The noun надежда takes на too.

RU-B1-13-013.notes: сердиться на + accusative: на меня. Не сердись is the imperfective negative imperative. The perfective is рассердиться.

RU-B1-13-014.notes: участвовать в + prepositional: в конкурсе. принимать участие в is a more formal synonym. The noun участие takes в too.

RU-B1-13-015.notes: привыкнуть к + dative: к новой работе. The future привыкнешь is perfective. The imperfective is привыкать.

RU-B1-13-016.notes: относиться к + dative means 'feel about, have an attitude to': к этому. It's the standard way to ask for an opinion.

RU-B1-13-017.notes: скучать по + dative means 'miss': скучаю по тебе. With мы and вы, по нам and по вам are now standard; по нас and по вас are older forms and still heard.
